lead: she says it across her own kitchen — he'll take you — to her son, who turns round and looks at you, and that was the whole of how it was arranged, the first time and every time since.
sun: and you do take him. the appointment at the far end of the county, the interview nobody in his house knows how to prepare for, the first morning of the job — you go the distance with each one and turn round in a car park. it works every time, which is the reason the sentence keeps getting said in kitchens you are not in.
moon: nothing in you was ever asked, because nothing in you was ever going to refuse, and a saturday with nothing written on it is where other people's logistics go. by now it is furnished: three families keep your name in their calendars in handwriting other than yours, and the account they give of it is that you love doing this and would be lost without it.
pull: nobody ever asked you. what got filled was a saturday, and the version everybody works from now is that you offered, warmly, in a kitchen you were only passing through.
tension: no agreement exists to get out of, which is what makes getting out of it impossible. one saturday you cannot do reads, in three houses at once, as a decision taken against a nineteen-year-old, and any account you gave of how the arrangement began would land as resentment of children who have done nothing to you. so nothing gets said, and the list grows by one household roughly every other year.
cost: the clearing happens first — the day goes blank before anybody has said what for — which is why somebody who would get into a car with nobody else got to the far side of a bad two years. nobody had to ask, and nobody can now stop. the clearing runs ahead of any request, so the requests stopped coming years back and the saturdays did not.

lead: the worst of it came out sideways in a queue at a housing office, without him stopping walking, because you were the one taking him and would not be there afterwards.
sun: the work is ordinary and it is all logistics: the deposit, the phone, the first shift, the daughter who has to be written to before she can be rung. six months, with an ending already fixed in them, which both of you knew on the first morning. that is why the talking is possible at all. a man tells the whole of it to somebody who is timetabled to be gone.
moon: all of it lands, unsorted — in cars, in corridors, at bus stops, in the flat gaps between one office and the next. no part of you screens what comes in, so what you hold of each man is his own complete version, given while he was in motion and had no settled life yet to keep it out of.
pull: men tell you everything because you are timetabled to leave. the leaving happens on schedule. what they said does not go with you, and cannot be handed to the people who have him now.
tension: when one of them goes under, four years on, the people around him are working from the short version and cannot see it coming until it has come. you can hear it in a phone call. saying so means producing something a man told you in a corridor before any of them knew him, which he has since decided not to be, and which he would be entitled to deny.
cost: he has a flat, a job and a daughter who rings him, and none of that would have arrived without somebody who could be told the disqualifying thing in week one and not flinch. the far side is where you are no longer cleared to know it. each of them is the author of a life that leaves out the person who heard the rest.

lead: somewhere in another city a woman asks for what she needs at exactly your speed, with your pauses in it, and the room she is asking answers her, and none of that has your name in it.
sun: what she is being taken to is a room she can go into by herself, so the route is made of specifics: the sentence she will need on the phone, the pause that stops a man talking over her. you go with her the first four times and wait outside on the fifth, and the fifth is the whole point. there is nowhere further to take her after that.
moon: the route does not survive the arrival. the beat does. she took her timing off you — where the pause goes, how fast to come back at somebody, the rate that makes a hard sentence land — and carried it into a life you have no part of. it was set for one frightened year. it is running now in an interview and a marriage.
pull: routes do not survive arrival. a cadence does — chosen inside one frightened year, running tonight in a voice that has never wondered where its timing came from.
tension: four of yours in a row, and the person listening hears one person — that gets said at the centre, half joking, and it is accurate. it cannot be helped from here, because the alternative was sending somebody into a language that punishes hesitation with no rhythm at all. the arrived ones are out of reach. the ones halfway there need this week to sound like last week.
cost: two years without speaking in a room, and then a phone call taken in company that went well — the difference was a rate somebody had put in his mouth. rates persist. forty people are carrying a timing chosen for the hardest year of their lives, and the ones it no longer suits are being corrected, gently, by teachers who have never heard of you.

lead: eleven have taken up an offer that is genuine, open and said out loud, and each was on the road inside a fortnight, thanking you, having come for a rest.
sun: what arrives at yours is a person with nothing arranged and nowhere to be, and inside a month there is a route. nothing was proposed to them — you are out ahead of it, ringing whoever does the paperwork, going with them on the wednesday, waiting outside. the welcome was real, and it converts every time into distance covered. they came for a rest and are travelling by the third week.
moon: the welcome has nothing attached to it — no requirement, no clock, no version of you that will get tired of them. what it does not include is a place to remain. the opening becomes a direction almost immediately, so a person who came to sit down for a year finds themselves being taken somewhere by somebody who has not hurried them for a single day.
pull: what gets offered is a place to be, and what gets delivered is distance, and everybody who has taken it needed the second one and had asked for the first.
tension: you cannot just sit with people is the complaint, and it arrives from the ones who like you most, usually after they have been through it themselves. no reduced version of it exists, so a friend who wanted an evening of nothing gets an evening of nothing and then a phone number by ten. it is heard as generosity by everybody it worked on, and as something harder by the two it did not.
cost: a year of doing nothing at yours is the one thing on offer that nobody has ever received. the people who came flattened are somewhere else now and glad of it, and each arrived on an invitation taken at face value. the welcome is genuine, and the second half of it is a road, and you have never managed to hand over only the first half.
